sources.title: Selma Lagerlof (Q44519), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-31): label 'Selma Lagerlof', description 'Swedish writer (1858-1940)', born 20 November 1858, died 16 March 1940, Korean label present. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.
Wikipedia, 'Selma Lagerlof', fetched for orientation (dates, Academy membership, the existence of her suffrage speeches). Orientation only; never counted as support for any row.

NobelPrize.org, 'Selma Lagerlof - Biographical' (the biography written at the time of the 1909 award and republished in Nobel Lectures), read in full: trained as a teacher, taught at the girls' secondary school in Landskrona from 1885, published nothing until a 1890 weekly's prize competition, Gosta Berlings Saga (1891) went unnoticed until its Danish translation was acclaimed, in 1895 support from the royal family and the Swedish Academy encouraged her to give up teaching, then Jerusalem (1901-02), Nils Holgersson (1906) and the later trilogy and Marbacka memoirs. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the prize body's own contemporaneous account; favourable by nature.

NobelPrize.org, 'Selma Lagerlof - Facts' (2026), read in full: gives the prize motivation ('lofty idealism, vivid imagination and spiritual perception'), says her debut novel broke away from the then-prevailing realism and naturalism, that her writing is rooted in folk tales and legends of her home district, and that the prize money let her buy back the family estate Marbacka. Institutional summary, favourable by nature.

NobelPrize.org, presentation speech for the 1909 Nobel Prize in Literature, read in full: a contemporary account for the Swedish Academy of why she was chosen, noting that Gosta Berlings Saga broke with the 'false realism' of the time yet was criticised severely by some, praising Jerusalem and The Girl from the Marsh Croft, and naming the Academy's gold medal of 1904. Speech by a member of the body that chose her, so admiring and not independent of the award.

NobelPrize.org, list of women Nobel Prize laureates, read: chronological list in which Selma Lagerlof (Literature, 1909) is the earliest woman shown for the Literature prize, with later literature laureates such as Grazia Deledda (1926) following. Used only to support the statement that she was the first woman awarded the Literature prize.

Svenskt kvinnobiografiskt lexikon, 'Selma Ottilia Lovisa Lagerlof' (article by Lisbeth Stenberg, 2018; in Swedish), read in full: a scholarly biography of her path from the Landskrona teaching post to full-time writing, the stylistic break of Gosta Berlings saga from 1880s realism, the harsh reviews from Carl David af Wirsen and Karl Warburg and the support of Georg Brandes, her field research for Jerusalem, the long preparation and travels for Nils Holgersson, the buying back of Marbacka, her membership of the Swedish Academy from 1914 and that she never stopped writing. Independent scholarly lexicon; its political and personal-life parts were not used.

Svenskt biografiskt lexikon, 'Selma O L Lagerlof' (article by Ying Toijer-Nilsson, 1977-79; in Swedish), read in full: the national biographical dictionary's entry, with her career dates and honours (Swedish Academy member from 1914), the observation that she habitually worked up modest material imaginatively, her trips to Nas and Jerusalem for the novel, the thorough rewrite of its second part for the 1909 edition, and how the harsh criticism of Wirsen, set against Brandes's praise, made her known but also unsure and tentative. Independent scholarly reference; some personal-life remarks were not used.

Marbacka foundation site, 'Entreprenoren' page (in Swedish), read in full: describes how she ran the estate commercially after returning, with an apple orchard, kitchen and herb gardens, a shop, a mechanised farm and, for a period, the oat-flour company Marbacka Havremjol (sold in Stockholm and exported to the United States), which did not become the success she had hoped, after which she added a bakery. Estate-foundation page named for her, so self-affiliated and admiring; used only for dated activities.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_lagerlof_skbl, src_lagerlof_sbl, src_lagerlof_nobelfacts, src_lagerlof_nobelspeech | 1889-1907 | scholarly lexicons + prize body] The Swedish women's biographical lexicon says that in spring 1889 she found her own lyrical, rhythmic prose, a break with the 'grey-weather realism' of the 1880s; the Nobel pages and the 1909 presentation speech likewise describe Gosta Berlings Saga as breaking with the realism of its time and as strikingly original. The reception was split, with Wirsen and Warburg scornful and Brandes enthusiastic, which tests the novelty claim against contemporaries rather than only against later praise. Original style and material is documented; most support is institutional admiration, so confidence is moderate.

persistence.rationale: [src_lagerlof_skbl, src_lagerlof_sbl, src_lagerlof_nobelbio | 1886-1940 | scholarly lexicons + prize body] After a debut that drew mixed and in places scornful reviews she kept teaching and writing, experimenting with style and subject in many short stories until she could live on her writing in 1895, and the Swedish women's lexicon says she never stopped writing, still working on new stories in January 1940. A long working life is documented across two scholarly sources and the prize body; no source describes her daily routine, so the score stays moderate.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_lagerlof_skbl, src_lagerlof_sbl | 1899-1909 | scholarly lexicons] Both lexicons say Jerusalem rested on real events in Nas parish, and that she studied them thoroughly, travelling to Nas and to Jerusalem; the women's lexicon adds that Nils Holgerssons underbara resa required a long preparation and many journeys, and the national dictionary records a thorough rewrite of the novel's second part for the 1909 edition after neither critics nor author were satisfied. Two scholarly sources describe deliberate research and revision, but they do not describe her own account of her working method and the examples are few.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_lagerlof_marbacka, src_lagerlof_skbl, src_lagerlof_nobelfacts | 1907-1930s | estate foundation + scholarly lexicon + prize body] The Nobel Facts page and the women's lexicon say she bought back the family estate Marbacka in 1907 and used the prize to regain the whole property; the estate foundation describes how she then ran it commercially, with an orchard, a shop, mechanised farming and an oat-flour company that did not succeed as hoped, after which she added a bakery. Initiative beyond writing is documented, including an uneven result, but the business detail comes mainly from the foundation's own page. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 because the business detail comes from the estate foundation's own page, which itself records that the oat-flour venture fell short, and no independent source assesses it.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_lagerlof_sbl, src_lagerlof_skbl | 1891-1895 | scholarly lexicons] The national dictionary says the sharply divided criticism of her debut, with Wirsen's attack the best known, made her known but also unsure and tentative, and that she answered by arguing that nearly everything in the book had a basis in reality; the women's lexicon adds that her mentors' defence of her probably only hardened the critics' resistance. This shows a documented defensive and uncertain response to hostile reviews early in her career, but she kept experimenting and writing, and one early episode from two lexicons is thin evidence of how she handled later conflict, so the score is held near the middle and the impact is dual_edged.

provenance.notes:
portrait_preflight: plausible (lead) / the lead's file (Atelier Jaeger, 'Atelje Jaeger - Selma Lagerlof 1928.jpeg', 2492 x 3509) was REJECTED: its Commons licence statement says the photographer is unknown (studio owner Herman Sylwander 1883-1948 or an assistant), the date is disputed (1922 or 1928) and gives only a Swedish-photo PD tag, with no documented US basis or publication record and a press-image source (marbacka.com); an unknown or possibly Sylwander-authored studio portrait is not a rights basis I can state concretely. REPLACEMENT USED: Commons file 'Selma Lagerlof by Goodwin 1917.png' (source: Alvin, Uppsala University Library), photograph by the Swedish photographer Henry B. Goodwin (born 20 February 1878, died 11 September 1931; Wikidata Q2565745 and Swedish Wikipedia; Goodwin's Konstnarsportratt of 1917 and other sources list Lagerlof among his portrait subjects; the print is signed 'Goodwin' at the lower left, as seen on the downloaded file). Rights basis: the creator died in 1931, so Swedish copyright (life plus 50 years until 1995, then 70) had expired by the end of 1981, well before the 1 January 1996 URAA date, so the work was already public domain in its source country and was not restored in the United States; this basis does not depend on whether or when the print was published. The Commons record gives the date as 1917, a Kungliga biblioteket copy in Commons is dated 1918 and a World Digital Library copy 1917-1920, so the year is approximate. Caveats: I could not open the Alvin item page (JavaScript portal) or the WDL page, so the attribution to Goodwin rests on the Commons record, the visible signature and the Goodwin biographies; the Alvin page was not checked for a stated usage rule. Original 3647 x 4576 PNG, downscaled to 956 x 1200 JPEG, no cropping, never upscaled. Other Commons candidates (Aron Jonason 1909, Anton Blomberg 1906, Bain) were looked at; the Jonason/Bain item is credited from a Library of Congress copy that I could not open. Why the lead's grade 'plausible' only partly held: the lead file's PD tag did not hold up under a concrete US analysis; a signed, named-creator alternative did.
